new.title: See the black paintings at the Musée Soulages
new.desc: The museum opened on 30 May 2014 and holds 514 works donated by Pierre Soulages, the painter of black who was born in Rodez. The Corten steel building was designed by the Catalan architects RCR and sits in the Jardin du Foirail.
new.tip: The ticket is also valid for the Musée Fenaille; check current hours on the museum website as they change by season.
new.q: Musée Soulages, Avenue Victor Hugo, Rodez

new.title: Admire the red sandstone Cathédrale Notre-Dame
new.desc: Work on the Gothic cathedral began in 1277 around the older Romanesque church, and it dominates the town from its hilltop. The fortress-like pink sandstone west front once formed part of the ramparts, and the 87-metre bell tower was built between 1513 and 1526.
new.tip: Visit in the afternoon when the light warms the sandstone, then look at the stained glass and the organ case inside. Entry is free.
new.q: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Rodez, Place de la Cité, Rodez

new.title: Meet the prehistoric statue-menhirs at Musée Fenaille
new.desc: The museum in the Hôtel de Jouéry shows seventeen statue-menhirs, the largest collection in France of large prehistoric human figures. The best known is the Dame de Saint-Sernin, about 5,000 years old, and the museum opened in 1937 thanks to the industrialist Maurice Fenaille.
new.tip: Combined ticket with the Musée Soulages. Allow about an hour.
new.q: Musée Fenaille, Place Raynaldy, Rodez

new.title: Spot the carved medallions of the Maison d'Armagnac
new.desc: This Renaissance merchant's house was built in the second quarter of the 16th century and classified as a historic monument in 1862. Its medallions were once read as the counts of Armagnac, hence the name, but it actually belonged to the merchant Hugues Daulhou.
new.tip: The house is admired from outside only; combine it with the nearby Place du Bourg and Église Saint-Amans.
new.q: Maison d'Armagnac, Place de l'Olmet, Rodez

new.title: Look up at the medieval Tour Corbières
new.desc: This 15th-century watchtower is one of the roughly twenty that once studded the medieval ramparts of Rodez. It was turned into a prison during the French Revolution and stands beside the bishop's palace.
new.tip: Visible from the outside only, on Boulevard d'Estourmel, a short stroll from the cathedral.
new.q: Tour Corbières, Boulevard d'Estourmel, Rodez

new.title: Step into Église Saint-Amans, the baroque church of the Bourg
new.desc: The church stands on the burial site of Saint Amans, traditionally the first bishop of Rodez, and was rebuilt in the 18th century with a baroque exterior and neo-Romanesque interior. It has been a listed monument since 1943 and keeps the reliquary bust of the saint.
new.tip: It sits in the Bourg quarter next to Place du Bourg; entry is free.
new.q: Église Saint-Amans, Rodez

new.title: Browse sculpture at the Musée Denys-Puech
new.desc: The fine arts museum was founded by the sculptor Denys Puech (1854-1942) and opened around 1910 in a building by André Boyer. It holds 306 works by Puech and shows artists from the Aveyron plus contemporary exhibitions.
new.tip: Entry has been listed as free; it is usually open Wednesday to Sunday afternoons outside summer, so check before you go.
new.q: Musée des Beaux-Arts Denys-Puech, Place Georges Clemenceau, Rodez

new.title: Stroll the Jardin du Foirail and its 1894 bandstand
new.desc: The garden was a livestock fairground from the 17th century and became a public garden in the 19th century. It contains a cast-iron octagonal bandstand from 1894, a war memorial moved in 2014, and the Musée Soulages.
new.tip: A free park, best combined with a visit to the Soulages museum or a coffee at Café Bras.
new.q: Jardin du Foirail, Avenue Victor Hugo, Rodez

new.title: Lunch at Café Bras inside the Musée Soulages
new.desc: The Bras family runs this restaurant in the museum, with a snack counter for tarts and a restaurant with a market-led menu using Aveyron produce. It is listed in the Michelin Guide and Gault&Millau scores it 13/20.
new.tip: Lunch menu around 43-45 euros; dinner only on Saturday. Book ahead and check opening days as it is closed some weekdays.
new.q: Café Bras, Jardin du Foirail, Avenue Victor Hugo, Rodez

new.title: Order farçous and aligot at L'Aubrac Café
new.desc: This restaurant on Place de la Cité, facing the cathedral, serves regional classics including farçous, regional charcuterie, aligot, tête de veau and chou farci. Gault&Millau describes it as a classic local address that keeps to regional tradition.
new.tip: Ask for the farçous as a starter and aligot with sausage as the main dish.
new.q: L'Aubrac Café, 8 Place de la Cité, Rodez

new.title: Try the salade aux farçous at Le Lion d'Or
new.desc: A family restaurant on the Avenue de Paris, known for its farçous salad with homemade farçous, the herb and chard fritters of the Rouergue. The menu also lists lamb sweetbreads in persillade and fish grills.
new.tip: The place seats about 100 and has affordable set menus; book at weekends.
new.q: Le Lion d'Or, 89 Avenue de Paris, Rodez

new.title: Eat a steak or local plate at La Gargouille by the cathedral
new.desc: This bistro-brasserie stands on Place d'Estaing right beside the cathedral, with about 35 seats inside and a large terrace. Reviewers praise its steaks and regional plates that include farçous and Tomme gratin.
new.tip: Take a terrace table facing the cathedral; reservations help in summer.
new.q: La Gargouille, 1 Place d'Estaing, Rodez

new.title: Book a star table at Restaurant Hervé Busset
new.desc: Hervé Busset holds a Michelin star and is described as the only starred restaurant in Rodez. It stands on the Place du Bourg in the old town and focuses on refined cooking with Aveyron produce.
new.tip: A gastronomic splurge; reserve in advance and check the current Michelin listing for distinctions.
new.q: Restaurant Hervé Busset, 24 Place du Bourg, Rodez

new.title: Buy a Mandarelle cake at Pâtisserie Clément
new.desc: A well-known pastry and chocolate shop in the old town, recommended by Gault&Millau. Its regional travel cake, the Mandarelle, combines apple, hazelnut and chestnut cream.
new.tip: Take a Mandarelle away as a picnic cake; it is on rue d'Armagnac near the Maison d'Armagnac.
new.q: Pâtisserie Clément, 3 rue d'Armagnac, Rodez

new.title: Browse the Saturday market around Place du Bourg
new.desc: The weekly market fills the old town on Saturday mornings, around Place du Bourg, Place Emma Calvé and rue Frayssinous. Stalls sell local cheeses, charcuterie, produce and Aveyron specialities.
new.tip: Come before noon; the market has been moving back to Place de la Cité, so check the current layout with the town hall.
new.q: Place du Bourg, Rodez

new.title: Walk the Panoramique de Rodez loop
new.desc: A signposted 9 km loop of about 2h45 and 350 m of climbing that gives views of Rodez on its hilltop above the Aveyron valley. It mixes lanes, paths and steps.
new.tip: Wear shoes that can get muddy in autumn and winter, and keep energy for the last climb. The start is 1.8 km from the station.
new.q: Panoramique de Rodez, Place de la Cité, Rodez

new.title: Follow the historic centre discovery circuit
new.desc: A signposted walking circuit links the cathedral, the Bourg quarter, the Maison d'Armagnac and the medieval streets. The route passes the Jesuit college chapel, whose exterior can be seen from Place Foch.
new.tip: Start at Place de la Cité and allow about two hours; the Jardin du Foirail makes a good end point.
new.q: Place de la Cité, Rodez

new.title: Read the Last Judgment on the Conques abbey tympanum
new.desc: The Romanesque abbey church of Sainte-Foy has a west portal tympanum showing the Last Judgment, dated about 1120-1140, with Christ flanked by paradise and hell. Conques sits on the Way of St James via Le Puy.
new.tip: Entry to the church is free; evening visits with the organ and lights are atmospheric. Allow time for the cloister and village lanes.
new.q: Abbatiale Sainte-Foy, Conques-en-Rouergue

new.title: See the golden Majesté in the Conques treasury
new.desc: The treasury holds the richest group of medieval goldsmith work in France. Its masterpiece is the reliquary statue of Sainte-Foy, made of gold plates on a wooden core and set with gems and antique cameos.
new.tip: Open every day of the year except 25 December and 1 January; tickets are around 6.50 euros. Hours are roughly 9:30-12:30 and 14:00-18:30 in summer.
new.q: Trésor de Conques, Rue Charlemagne, Conques-en-Rouergue

new.title: Gaze at the Millau Viaduct from the Aire du Viaduc
new.desc: The Site du Viaduc de Millau at Brocuéjouls has a belvédère open at all hours, a Viaduc Expo and an Espace Gourmand. The view over the cable-stayed bridge across the Tarn valley is described by reviewers as exceptional.
new.tip: Reach it from the A75 exit 45 or by the D911 from Millau. Entry to the site is free during 2026.
new.q: Site du Viaduc de Millau, Brocuéjouls, Millau

new.title: Cross the Gothic bridge at Estaing
new.desc: The village hugs a rocky promontory above the Lot, topped by the château of the Estaing family, owned by a foundation tied to Valéry Giscard d'Estaing's family since 2012. Its Gothic bridge dates from the late 15th or early 16th century and is part of the Camino de Santiago UNESCO listing.
new.tip: Join a guided visit of the village and château, or canoe the Lot below the bridge.
new.q: Pont d'Estaing, Estaing

new.title: Cross the moat into Château de Belcastel
new.desc: A medieval fortress overlooking the Aveyron river and its village, restored in the 20th century by the architect Fernand Pouillon. Visits are self-guided with a leaflet or audio guide through the moat, the castle and its gardens.
new.tip: Open from April to November, adult ticket about 10 euros in 2026; the village below is among the prettiest in the Aveyron.
new.q: Château de Belcastel, Belcastel

new.title: Climb the keep of Najac's royal fortress
new.desc: The fortress crowns a ridge above the Aveyron gorge, and the village below runs along the crest. Visitors praise the view from the keep and the spiral staircase, and entry is from about 7 euros.
new.tip: Wear comfortable shoes for steep streets and stairs; both guided and free visits are offered.
new.q: Forteresse royale de Najac, Rue du Château, Najac

new.title: Climb the belfry of Villefranche's Collégiale Notre-Dame
new.desc: The collegiate church was started around 1260, a few years after the bastide was founded, and finished with a belfry at the end of the 15th century. The belfry has 163 steps, and the arcaded Place Notre-Dame is a near-intact bastide square.
new.tip: The church is free to visit; the belfry is by guided or free visit. Thursday morning is market day on the square.
new.q: Collégiale Notre-Dame, Place Notre-Dame, Villefranche-de-Rouergue

new.title: Walk the arcades of Sauveterre-de-Rouergue
new.desc: This royal bastide village, a member of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, was founded around 1281. Its central square measures about 60 by 40 metres and is lined with 47 arcades.
new.tip: Sunday morning is market day on the square; a candlelit festival is held on the second Saturday of August.
new.q: Place des Arcades, Sauveterre-de-Rouergue

new.title: Walk the ramparts of La Couvertoirade Templar village
new.desc: A fortified village built by the Knights Templar and then the Hospitallers on the Larzac plateau, with ramparts raised by the Hospitallers in the 15th century and classified since 1895. The walk on the ramparts covers about half of the fortifications.
new.tip: Visit from about 3 euros, audio guide extra; parking is paid. In summer there are guided tours at 11:00, 15:00 and 17:00.
new.q: La Couvertoirade, cité templière

new.title: Visit the Cistercian Abbaye de Sylvanès
new.desc: A Cistercian abbey now known as a centre for sacred and world music and architecture. The Romanesque and Gothic buildings host a festival each summer.
new.tip: Individual visits start from about 3 euros, but there are no visits on the afternoons of festival concerts. Phone 05 65 98 20 20 for times.
new.q: Abbaye de Sylvanès, Sylvanès

new.title: Wander the cliff-hugging village of Peyre
new.desc: Peyre is a former commune, now part of Comprégnac, and a member of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France. Its houses are built against a steep cliff pierced by caves on the Tarn near Millau.
new.tip: Nearby Comprégnac has a troglodytic church, Saint-Cristofol, listed since 1936. Park below the village and walk up.
new.q: Peyre, Comprégnac

new.title: Descend by funicular into the Aven Armand cave
new.desc: The cave on the Causse Méjean was found by Louis Armand in September 1897. A funicular installed in 1963 spares visitors a staircase of 360 steps, and the classic visit lasts about an hour.
new.tip: Book online. It is cool underground, so bring a layer even in July. There is also a two-hour exploration tour with rappel.
new.q: Aven Armand, Hures-la-Parade

new.title: Explore the rock city of Montpellier-le-Vieux
new.desc: A 120-hectare chaos of dolomite rocks on the Causse Noir, in the commune of La Roque-Sainte-Marguerite east of Millau. Marked paths cross pines and oaks, and a small train offers a guided circuit of about an hour.
new.tip: The little train suits families and reduced mobility; check current hours and prices at the park entrance.
new.q: Chaos de Montpellier-le-Vieux, La Roque-Sainte-Marguerite

new.title: Visit the cathedral of Mende and its Saint Privat crypt
new.desc: The cathedral was begun around 1369 on the initiative of Pope Urban V, who came from the Gévaudan, and later got its two 16th-century bell towers. It is linked to Saint Privat, first bishop of the Gévaudan, whose tomb is in a crypt below.
new.tip: The main bell tower can be climbed for a fee. The cathedral stands on Place Urbain V in the town centre.
new.q: Cathédrale Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Privat, Place Urbain V, Mende

new.title: Climb the Porte du Soubeyran in Marvejols
new.desc: The 14th-century gate with two thick towers is one of three medieval gates left from Marvejols' ramparts. A statue of the Beast of Gévaudan and one of Henri IV flank it, and the climb of 68 steps gives a view over the old rooftops.
new.tip: A small archaeological museum is inside; the gate is protected as a historic monument.
new.q: Porte du Soubeyran, Marvejols

new.title: Look into the horseshoe canyon of Bozouls
new.desc: The Trou de Bozouls is a horseshoe-shaped gorge 400 m across and over 100 m deep, cut by the Dourdou, with the village perched on its rim. Viewpoints in the village and paths down to the river make it easy to see.
new.tip: Access is free. The two marked loops of about 2 km and 4 km take roughly 1 to 1.5 hours.
new.q: Trou de Bozouls, Bozouls

new.title: Admire the twisted spire of Saint-Côme-d'Olt
new.desc: The church of Saint-Côme et Saint-Damien has a helical spire 18 metres high from the early 16th century, rebuilt after lightning strikes in 1627 and later. The circular village on the GR65 is classed among the most beautiful villages of France.
new.tip: The village is a stage on the Way of St James; a loop around the ring street takes under an hour.
new.q: Église Saint-Côme et Saint-Damien, Saint-Côme-d'Olt

new.title: Look down the Gorges du Tarn from the Point Sublime
new.desc: The viewpoint stands at 870 m on the Causse de Sauveterre, over 400 m above the river, in the commune of Le Massegros. It gives a classic panorama of the Tarn gorges between La Malène and Les Vignes.
new.tip: Reach it by the D46 from Les Vignes or the D32 and D146 from Le Massegros; a walk starts from the car park.
new.q: Point Sublime, Gorges du Tarn, Le Massegros

new.title: Wander Sainte-Énimie, village of the legendary princess
new.desc: The village grew from an abbey founded by Énimie after she was healed of leprosy at the Burle spring, according to the legend, and is a member of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France. A marked path of about 45 minutes to an hour climbs to the hermitage above the gorge.
new.tip: It is a good base for canoeing and hiking on the GR736; the former abbey area is above the village.
new.q: Sainte-Énimie, Gorges du Tarn Causses

new.title: Splurge on a tasting menu at Le Suquet in Laguiole
new.desc: Michel Bras created this glass-walled restaurant in 1992 on a promontory above Laguiole, and his son Sébastien now runs it. It is listed with two Michelin stars, and the cooking is built around Aubrac plants and produce.
new.tip: Reservations are essential and the dress is smart; check the seasonal opening days before planning.
new.q: Le Suquet, Route de l'Aubrac, Laguiole

new.title: Taste Laguiole AOP at the Jeune Montagne cheese dairy
new.desc: The cooperative at La Borie Neuve makes Laguiole AOP and Tome fraîche de l'Aubrac IGP from raw whole milk. The free visit lasts 30 to 45 minutes and includes a film, a glass gallery over production and a tasting.
new.tip: Cheese is made in the morning, so visit then. Phone 05 65 44 35 54 to confirm hours.
new.q: Coopérative fromagère Jeune Montagne, La Borie Neuve, Laguiole

new.title: Dine at the Auberge Saint-Jacques opposite Conques abbey
new.desc: A hotel-restaurant with the Table gastronomique label, facing the abbey church on rue Gonzague Florens. Gault&Millau lists it as a Table Gourmande, and the à la carte menu in 2026 runs roughly 5.50 to 28 euros.
new.tip: The terrace seats 18; call 05 65 72 86 36 to book, particularly in high season.
new.q: Auberge Saint-Jacques, 8 rue Gonzague Florens, Conques-en-Rouergue

new.title: Taste chef Rémy Simon's cooking at L'Oustal del Barry in Najac
new.desc: A hotel-restaurant on Place du Sol del Barry labelled Maître Restaurateur, Table gastronomique and one toque. The chef, Rémy Simon, makes everything in-house, using regional ingredients.
new.tip: Reservations are required; one guide says the restaurant is closed on winter evenings from November to March.
new.q: L'Oustal del Barry, 2 place du Sol del Barry, Najac

new.title: Eat aligot made at your table at the Buron des Bouals
new.desc: A traditional stone buron near Saint-Chély-d'Aubrac that serves aligot made in front of diners, with sausage. It stands about 800 m from the village on the road toward Nasbinals, with a view over the Aubrac.
new.tip: Menus are around 13 to 19 euros; confirm opening dates as the burons are seasonal.
new.q: Buron des Bouals, 448 chemin des Bouals, Saint-Chély-d'Aubrac

new.title: Taste fouace and flaune at Pâtisserie Saint-Jacques in Millau
new.desc: A bakery on Place du Mandarous that Lonely Planet lists among the best in Millau, serving the fouace (orange-blossom brioche) and the flaune, a tart of sheep's cheese and orange blossom. It has a 4.8 rating from 46 reviews on Petit Futé.
new.tip: Buy a fouace to take away; the Wednesday and Friday market is nearby.
new.q: Pâtisserie Saint-Jacques, Place du Mandarous, Millau

new.title: Taste Marcillac wine at Domaine du Cros
new.desc: Philippe Teulier and his son Julien run this 34-hectare estate in Goutrens, a key name in the Marcillac appellation, which makes red wine from the Fer Servadou grape. The family has farmed here since 1882.
new.tip: Visits and tastings cost about 4 to 6 euros, with a free simple tasting; call 05 65 72 71 77 to make an appointment.
new.q: Domaine du Cros, 709 route du Cros, Goutrens

new.title: Eat aligot at Les Voûtes in Mende
new.desc: A restaurant in Mende serving traditional cuisine, with aligot, regional meats and duck breast. The menu changes every three months.
new.tip: Check opening days before going; Mende's cathedral is a short walk away.
new.q: Les Voûtes, Mende

new.title: Try pélardon ravioli at L'Adonis in Florac
new.desc: Chef Martial Paulet cooks seasonal dishes at this restaurant on rue du Pêcher, including ravioli with Cévennes pélardon cheese and Ance brown trout fillets. Gault&Millau scores it 13/20.
new.tip: Listed as open from 3 April to 31 October 2026; check before visiting.
new.q: Restaurant L'Adonis, 48 rue du Pêcher, Florac Trois Rivières

new.title: Eat Roquefort burger and crème brûlée at Le Combalou
new.desc: This restaurant at Lauras, minutes from Roquefort-sur-Soulzon, has a menu with Roquefort crème brûlée, aligot with sausage and a Roquefort burger with homemade chips. It is listed as open all through 2026.
new.tip: Combine it with a cave visit at Roquefort Société or Papillon.
new.q: Restaurant Le Combalou, Lauras, Roquefort-sur-Soulzon

new.title: Order saucisse-aligot at the Hôtel de l'Europe in Marvejols
new.desc: The restaurant of this Logis hotel on place du Barry names saucisse-aligot, Aubrac beef and Lozère trout among its specialities. Set menus run from about 13 to 35 euros.
new.tip: Call 04 66 47 16 35 to book.
new.q: Hôtel de l'Europe, 11 place du Barry, Marvejols

new.title: Taste Marcillac wine at the Cave coopérative Le Vallon
new.desc: The cooperative of the Vignerons du Rougier de Marcillac, on the RD840 in Valady, has a space dedicated to Marcillac wine. The AOP red is made from Fer Servadou, known locally as Mansois.
new.tip: A handy stop between Rodez and Conques; check opening hours with the cooperative.
new.q: Cave coopérative Le Vallon, RD 840, Valady

new.title: Glide down the Gorges du Tarn by boat from La Malène
new.desc: The Bateliers des Gorges du Tarn run flat-bottomed boats of up to six passengers over about 8 km from La Malène to the Cirque des Baumes. A boatman narrates the geology and history, and a shuttle returns passengers to La Malène.
new.tip: The season runs from April to early November, and prices start around 27 euros; booking ahead is recommended.
new.q: Les Bateliers des Gorges du Tarn, La Malène

new.title: Tour the maturing caves of Roquefort Société
new.desc: A guided hour inside the natural caves under Roquefort-sur-Soulzon where Roquefort AOP ripens, ending with a tasting of the house cheeses. More than 100,000 visitors come each year to a working production site.
new.tip: Tickets start around 8 euros; an affineur-led visit with wine pairings costs from about 37 euros. Visites are possible all year.
new.q: Caves Roquefort Société, Avenue François Galtier, Roquefort-sur-Soulzon

new.title: Visit the Roquefort Papillon caves with a free tasting
new.desc: A one-hour guided tour of the cellars with a short documentary in French and English and a personalised tasting of the range at no charge. Paid formats include a 45-minute visit and a 1h30 sensory workshop with cheese and wine pairings.
new.tip: Booking by phone is advised, though walk-ins have been possible according to reviewers.
new.q: Les Caves Papillon, 8 bis avenue de Lauras, Roquefort-sur-Soulzon

new.title: Watch a Laguiole knife being assembled at the Forge
new.desc: The Forge de Laguiole was founded in 1987 to revive the Laguiole knife in its home village. The workshop can be visited freely for no charge year-round, and in July and August free guided tours show the assembly of a folding knife.
new.tip: Guided tours run Monday to Friday in July and August (about 50 minutes). Check hours as sources differ on Saturday opening.
new.q: Coutellerie Forge de Laguiole, Route de l'Aubrac, Laguiole

new.title: Watch wolves at the Parc des Loups du Gévaudan
new.desc: The park in the Margeride hills holds roughly 100 wolves from several origins in semi-liberty and has a museum on wolf myths, including the Beast of Gévaudan. It opened to visitors in 1985.
new.tip: Admission was listed at about 16 euros for adults and 13 for ages 3 to 11; dogs are not allowed.
new.q: Parc des Loups du Gévaudan, Sainte-Lucie, Saint-Léger-de-Peyre

new.title: Hike the canyon loops of Bozouls from the medieval towers
new.desc: Two marked loops of about 2 km and 4 km, taking 1 to 1.5 hours with 200 m of climb, descend to the Dourdou and cross footbridges below the cliffs of the Trou de Bozouls. A 2 km Bacambou loop starts at the medieval towers.
new.tip: Follow the yellow waymarks; the footbridges replace fords that are often under water.
new.q: Tours médiévales, Bozouls

new.title: Hike from Nasbinals to the Cascade du Déroc
new.desc: A walk across the Aubrac plateau to a 32 m waterfall fed by the outlet of the Lac des Salhiens, falling from a basalt cliff. The classic loop is about 10 km and 3h30 with 159 m of climb.
new.tip: An easier 6.9 km route exists; take a map such as IGN 2537 OT. Park on the main square of Nasbinals.
new.q: Place de Nasbinals, Nasbinals

new.title: Climb the Pic de Finiels on Mont Lozère
new.desc: At 1,699 m, the Sommet de Finiels is the highest point of the Cévennes. Routes start from the Col de Finiels, from the hamlet of Finiels, or from the Le Bleymard ski station at 1,416 m.
new.tip: Allow around 4 to 5 hours; the GR70 passes near the summit. Check the route and weather before leaving.
new.q: Col de Finiels, Mont Lozère

new.title: Swim at the Lac de Naussac beach near Langogne
new.desc: The beach near the village of Naussac is a supervised swimming spot on a reservoir shared by Langogne and Naussac-Fontanes. A nautical base also offers boating, and sailing regattas are held regularly.
new.tip: Supervision is seasonal, and water quality information was not available for 2026, so check on site.
new.q: Plage du lac de Naussac, Langogne

new.title: Browse the Thursday market in Villefranche's bastide square
new.desc: The big market fills the arcaded Place Notre-Dame on Thursday mornings, with regional specialities such as aligot and farçous. A smaller market is held on Saturday mornings under the Consulat arcades.
new.tip: Go between about 7:30 and noon; confirm schedule with the tourist office.
new.q: Place Notre-Dame, Villefranche-de-Rouergue

new.title: Watch griffon vultures at the Maison des Vautours
new.desc: A visitor centre in the Gorges de la Jonte at Le Truel, on the D996 between Le Rozier and Meyrueis, with a museum on vulture reintroduction and telescopes on a terrace. Vultures were reintroduced in the area from the 1970s.
new.tip: Adult tickets are around 7.90 euros; a 2025 listing showed Tuesday to Sunday 10:00-18:00 in April and the autumn, so check 2026 dates.
new.q: Maison des Vautours, Le Truel, Gorges de la Jonte

new.title: Hear concerts at the Sylvanès sacred and world music festival
new.desc: The Festival de Musiques Sacrées et du Monde held its 49th edition in 2026 at the abbey, from 12 July to 6 September. A few concerts take place in nearby towns including Millau, Saint-Affrique and Conques.
new.tip: Tickets are sold online with reduced fares for young people and jobseekers; abbey visits are not offered on concert afternoons.
new.q: Abbaye de Sylvanès, Sylvanès

new.title: Paddle the Tarn by canoe from Sainte-Énimie
new.desc: Canoë Méjean rents canoes and kayaks about 400 m from the village centre, with descents to Saint-Chély-du-Tarn (6 km) and La Malène (13 km). Prices start at about 19 euros, and the 2026 season runs from 8 May to 20 September.
new.tip: You need to swim; booking ahead is wise in July and August.
new.q: Canoë Méjean, Sainte-Énimie

new.title: Browse the Wednesday and Friday market on Place Foch
new.desc: The weekly market in Millau fills Place Foch and Place des Halles on Wednesdays and Fridays all year, from about 8:00 to 12:00. On Fridays it spreads into the adjacent streets up to the Halles.
new.tip: Buy Roquefort and fouace there; night markets of artisans are held on summer Wednesdays.
new.q: Place Foch, Millau

new.title: Fly a tandem paraglider over Millau and the viaduct
new.desc: Operators such as Air Magic Parapente offer tandem flights from sites including Pouncho d'Agast and Brunas, facing the viaduct, over the Parc des Grands Causses. A discovery flight costs from about 65 euros and a thrill flight about 120 euros.
new.tip: The take-off site depends on wind and weather; check the operator's age and weight limits.
new.q: Air Magic Parapente, 1207 B avenue de l'Aigoual, Millau

new.title: Walk the old town of Entraygues-sur-Truyère
new.desc: A signposted walking circuit of 21 numbered stops covers the old town at the confluence of the Lot and Truyère. It passes half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries, the castle and the medieval Truyère bridge.
new.tip: A visitor guide is available in French, English, Spanish, German and Dutch.
new.q: Vieille ville, Entraygues-sur-Truyère
